task: Lead a mixed-culture team: measure its health, set decision rules, plan meetings across time zones and arbitrate a conflict.
condition: Given a team profile, survey scores, work hours for three sites and a conflict case.
standard: Measures are calculated correctly, a decision rule fits the risk, the meeting plan has real overlap and the arbitration ends in a written agreement.
who: Team leaders and managers who work with people in several countries.

modules.title: How mixed teams form and stall
modules.intro: Teams from different countries pass through stages: meeting, friction, rules, then steady work. Cultural gaps often make the friction stage longer.
points: Expect friction and plan for it
Set shared rules early
Check the stage every month
modules.example: A team of 8 starts a project. After four weeks, a pulse check asks each person to rate 'we agree how we work' from 1 to 5. The scores are 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 2, 3, which total 22. The mean is 22 / 8 = 2.75. A score under 3.5 (an example cut-off) means the team is still in friction, so the lead holds a rules session before adding new tasks.
modules.activity: Run a five-question pulse check for a team of at least 6 and decide the stage from the mean.
modules.standard: The mean is calculated correctly and a stage and next step are named using a stated cut-off.

modules.title: Communication styles across cultures
modules.intro: Some teams say things directly and some hint. Neither is wrong, but a mismatch causes missed messages.
points: Direct and indirect styles
High and low context messages
Confirm meaning with a short read-back
modules.example: A manager from a direct culture writes 'This report is late.' A team member from an indirect culture hears it as a mild note, because in that culture a stronger sentence would be 'We must finish this today'. Of 10 recent deadline messages, 4 were missed by indirect speakers, a 40% miss rate. After a read-back rule (repeat the task and date in your own words), misses fall to 1 of 10, or 10%.
modules.activity: Take 10 past messages. Mark which were missed, add a read-back rule and compare the miss rate.
modules.standard: Miss rates before and after are shown as percentages and the rule is written in one sentence.

modules.title: Building trust at a distance
modules.intro: Trust comes from skill (I believe you can do it) and from personal ties (I know you care). Remote teams must build both on purpose.
points: Show reliable delivery
Share some personal background
Track promises kept
modules.example: A remote team logs promises made in weekly calls. In 4 weeks there were 48 promises and 39 were kept on time. The kept rate is 39 / 48 = 81%. One pair of members kept 6 of 12, which is 50%, so the lead meets them to find the cause. The team goal is 90%, which means at most 4 late promises in 48.
modules.activity: Log promises for two weeks for a team and work out the kept rate for the team and for one pair.
modules.standard: Both rates are correct and one action follows from the lowest figure.

modules.title: Meetings across time zones
modules.intro: Time zones cut the hours when people can meet. A fair plan rotates the inconvenient slot.
points: Find the overlap of working hours
Rotate the early and late slots
Record decisions in writing
modules.example: Three sites work 9:00 to 17:00. Site A is at UTC+1, site B at UTC+5:30 and site C at UTC-5. In UTC, A works 8:00 to 16:00, B works 3:30 to 11:30, C works 14:00 to 22:00. A and B overlap 8:00 to 11:30, which is 3.5 hours. All three never overlap. With three sites, a call at 14:00 UTC forces B to join at 19:30 local, so the slot rotates every month.
modules.activity: Take three cities and work out the daily overlap for each pair and name a rotation plan.
modules.standard: UTC conversion is shown, overlap hours are correct for each pair and a rotation plan is stated.

modules.title: Group decision rules
modules.intro: A team must know how it decides before it decides. Different cultures expect different rules, such as leader decides, vote, or talk until agreed.
points: Name the rule before the meeting
Match the rule to the risk
Record dissent
modules.example: A team of 7 must choose a supplier. Under majority rule, 4 votes are enough. Under a two-thirds rule, 7 x 2 / 3 = 4.67, so 5 votes are needed. Votes come in at 4 for supplier X and 3 for supplier Y. X wins under majority but fails the two-thirds rule. Because the contract is worth 2 million, the team chose two-thirds and held a second round.
modules.activity: Pick a decision rule for a team of 9 and state how many votes are needed for a majority and for two-thirds.
modules.standard: Majority is 5, two-thirds is 6, and the rule is matched to the size of the risk in writing.

modules.title: Types of conflict and how to read them
modules.intro: Conflict about the task is useful. Conflict about people drains a team. A lead must sort which is which before acting.
points: Task, process and relationship conflict
Sort each issue in a list
Act first on relationship harm
modules.example: A team lists 10 issues in a retro. 5 are about the task (design choices), 3 are about process (who approves) and 2 are about relationships (tone in chat). That is 50%, 30% and 20%. The 2 relationship issues are handled first in private talks. The task issues stay on the agenda because debate on them improves the design.
modules.activity: Collect 10 issues from a real or case team, sort them and give the percentage in each type.
modules.standard: Every issue is placed in one type, the percentages add to 100% and one first action is named.

modules.title: Arbitration steps
modules.intro: Arbitration is a structured process where a neutral person helps two sides reach a fair outcome. Each step has a time limit.
points: Hear each side with no interruption
List interests, not just demands
Test trades and write the deal
modules.example: Member A wants 14 days to finish a task and member B, who depends on it, needs it in 7. The arbiter asks for interests. A needs time for a data check, and B needs a first draft to start. The deal is a draft at day 7 and the checked version at day 12. That is 2 days less than A asked for and 5 days more than B asked for. Both sign a one-line note.
modules.activity: Run a mock arbitration with two sides who have different deadlines and write the agreed dates.
modules.standard: Interests are stated for both sides, the dates fall within the range of the two demands and both agree in writing.

modules.title: Measuring team health
modules.intro: A team should be measured, not guessed. A short survey every month shows trends before a crisis.
points: Use the same 5 questions each month
Track the trend, not one score
Act when the mean drops by more than 0.5
modules.example: Over three months, the mean trust score for a team is 4.1, 3.8 and 3.2. The drop from month 2 to month 3 is 0.6, which is above the 0.5 limit. The team has 8 people and 3 rated themselves 2 or less, which is 37.5%. The lead calls a session and sets a goal to get back to a mean of 3.8 within 6 weeks.
modules.activity: Take three monthly means and decide whether action is needed using the 0.5 rule.
modules.standard: The change is calculated correctly, the rule is applied and a goal with a date is set.

quiz.q: Five members rate team agreement 3, 4, 2, 5 and 4. What is the mean?
Site A is at UTC+2 and site B at UTC-3. Both work 9:00 to 17:00. What is their overlap?
quiz.a: A works 7:00 to 15:00 UTC, B works 12:00 to 20:00 UTC, so the overlap is 12:00 to 15:00, which is 3 hours.

quiz.q: A team kept 27 of 30 promises. What is the kept rate?
How many votes are a two-thirds majority in a team of 12?

quiz.a: Hearing the task repeated in the listener's own words shows whether the message was understood, even when the style is indirect.

quiz.q: Out of 20 issues, 6 are about relationships. What percentage is that?
What does an arbiter ask for after hearing both demands?
The trust mean falls from 4.0 to 3.4. Is action needed under a 0.5 rule?
quiz.a: Yes, because the drop is 0.6, which is above 0.5.

quiz.q: When a team is in friction after four weeks, what should the lead do first?
quiz.a: Hold a rules session on how the team works before adding new tasks.

quiz.q: Why rotate the inconvenient meeting slot?
quiz.a: So the same site does not always join at an unsocial hour, which keeps the load fair.

ladder.title: L1 Basic: Team stages
ladder.slide: A simple line shows meeting, friction, rules and steady work with the typical weeks for each.
ladder.notes: Say: friction is normal. Check: ask where the team sits now. Mistake: reading friction as failure.

ladder.title: L2 Basic: Styles of speaking
ladder.slide: Two sample messages say the same thing in a direct and an indirect way.
ladder.notes: Say: neither is wrong. Check: ask what each message means. Mistake: judging the indirect speaker as unclear.

ladder.title: L3 Core: Trust and promises
ladder.slide: A log shows promises made and kept with a kept rate.
ladder.notes: Say: count what is kept. Check: work out 18 of 24. Mistake: measuring friendliness instead of delivery.

ladder.title: L4 Core: Time zones
ladder.slide: A strip shows three work days in UTC with the overlap shaded.
ladder.notes: Say: convert to one clock first. Check: find the overlap. Mistake: forgetting daylight saving shifts.

ladder.title: L5 Applied: Decision rules
ladder.slide: A table lists majority, two-thirds and consensus with votes needed for 7 and 9 members.
ladder.notes: Say: pick the rule by the risk. Check: ask the votes for two-thirds of 9. Mistake: choosing the rule after the vote.

ladder.title: L6 Applied: Conflict sort and arbitration
ladder.slide: A list of issues is sorted into three types, followed by the four steps of arbitration.
ladder.notes: Say: sort, then act on relationship harm. Check: sort five sample issues. Mistake: giving a verdict instead of finding interests.

ladder.title: L7 Advanced: Team health over time
ladder.slide: A chart shows three monthly means and the 0.5 action line.
ladder.notes: Say: act on the trend. Check: ask what to do if the mean drops 0.7. Mistake: waiting for a visible crisis.

rubric.not_yet: Mean or rate is wrong or missing.
rubric.meets: Means and rates are correct with a stated cut-off.
rubric.exceeds: Also shows a trend and a goal with a date.

rubric.not_yet: Names a style gap but no fix.
rubric.meets: Adds a rule and shows the change in misses.
rubric.exceeds: Also tests the rule on a second case.

rubric.not_yet: Mixes up task and people issues.
rubric.meets: Sorts issues correctly and acts on relationship harm first.
rubric.exceeds: Also runs an arbitration that ends in a written deal.

rubric.meets: Overlap is correct and a rotation is set.
rubric.exceeds: Also weighs trade-offs for each site.

jobs.what: Leads mixed teams and runs rules sessions.
Plans meetings and decisions across sites.
Runs team surveys and reports trends.
